source_refs.note: Exercise 3.5, Question 15 (i)-(iv): show four integrals are zero (Properties IV, V); book pp. 102-103. No printed answer (show that).

blocks.explanation:
A 'show it is zero' question with no easy antiderivative.
Here \(a + b = \frac{\pi}{6} + \frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{\pi}{2}\); Property IV turns \(\tan x\) into \(\cot x\), and \(\ln \cot x = -\ln \tan x\).
So \(I = -I\).
steps:
Given: \(I = \int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} \ln(\tan x)\,dx\).
To prove: \(I = 0\).
Method: Property IV with \(a + b - x = \frac{\pi}{2} - x\), and \(\tan(\frac{\pi}{2} - x) = \cot x = \frac{1}{\tan x}\).

Apply Property IV
\[I = \int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} \ln\left(\tan\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2} - x\right)\right)dx\]
\[= \int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} \ln\left(\dfrac{1}{\tan x}\right)dx\]
Why: \(\frac{\pi}{6} + \frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{\pi}{2}\) and \(\tan(\frac{\pi}{2} - x) = \cot x\).

Use a log rule
\[\ln\dfrac{1}{\tan x} = -\ln(\tan x)\]
\[I = -\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3} \ln(\tan x)\,dx = -I\]
Why: \(\ln\frac{1}{p} = -\ln p\). On \([\frac{\pi}{6}, \frac{\pi}{3}]\), \(\tan x > 0\), so the log is defined.

Conclude
\[I = -I \Rightarrow 2I = 0 \Rightarrow I = 0\]
Why: a number equal to its negative is 0.

Check
\[\ln \tan\tfrac{\pi}{6} = -\tfrac{1}{2}\ln 3,\quad \ln \tan\tfrac{\pi}{3} = +\tfrac{1}{2}\ln 3\]
Why: the graph is negative on the left half and equally positive on the right half (mirror points \(x\) and \(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\)); a numerical evaluation gives 0.

blocks.prompt: 15 (ii) Show that: \(\int_{0}^{\pi} \frac{\sin x \cos x}{1 + e^{\sin x}}\,dx = 0\)
blocks.explanation:
Again 'show it is zero', with \(a + b = \pi\).
Under \(x \to \pi - x\): \(\sin x\) stays the same, \(\cos x\) changes sign. So the integrand changes sign.
Property IV gives \(I = -I\).
steps:
Given: \(I = \int_{0}^{\pi} \frac{\sin x \cos x}{1 + e^{\sin x}}\,dx\).
To prove: \(I = 0\).
Method: Property IV with \(x \to \pi - x\), using \(\sin(\pi - x) = \sin x\), \(\cos(\pi - x) = -\cos x\).

Apply Property IV
\[I = \int_{0}^{\pi} \dfrac{\sin(\pi - x)\cos(\pi - x)}{1 + e^{\sin(\pi - x)}}\,dx\]
\[= \int_{0}^{\pi} \dfrac{\sin x\,(-\cos x)}{1 + e^{\sin x}}\,dx\]
Why: \(0 + \pi - x = \pi - x\); the denominator does not change because it contains only \(\sin x\).

Compare
\[I = -\int_{0}^{\pi} \dfrac{\sin x \cos x}{1 + e^{\sin x}}\,dx = -I\]
Why: take the minus sign outside.

Conclude
\[2I = 0 \Rightarrow I = 0\]
Why: \(I = -I\).

Check
\[x = \tfrac{\pi}{4}:\ \cos x > 0;\quad x = \tfrac{3\pi}{4}:\ \cos x < 0\]
Why: points mirrored about \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) give equal and opposite values, so the areas cancel; a numerical evaluation gives 0.
blocks.final_answer: Hence proved: \(\int_{0}^{\pi} \frac{\sin x \cos x}{1 + e^{\sin x}}\,dx = 0\).

blocks.explanation:
\(a + b = \pi\) again. The factor \(x(\pi - x)\) does not change under \(x \to \pi - x\), but \(\cos(\pi - x)\) becomes \(\cos x = -\cos(\pi - x)\).
So Property IV gives \(I = -I\).
(The integral could also be done by parts, but this is much shorter.)
steps:
Given: \(I = \int_{0}^{\pi} x(\pi - x)\cos(\pi - x)\,dx\).
To prove: \(I = 0\).
Method: Property IV with \(x \to \pi - x\).

Apply Property IV
\[I = \int_{0}^{\pi} (\pi - x)\big(\pi - (\pi - x)\big)\cos\big(\pi - (\pi - x)\big)\,dx\]
\[= \int_{0}^{\pi} (\pi - x)\,x\,\cos x\,dx\]
Why: \(\pi - (\pi - x) = x\).

Compare with the original
\[\cos x = -\cos(\pi - x)\]
\[I = -\int_{0}^{\pi} x(\pi - x)\cos(\pi - x)\,dx = -I\]
Why: \(\cos(\pi - x) = -\cos x\), so \(\cos x = -\cos(\pi - x)\).

Conclude
\[2I = 0 \Rightarrow I = 0\]
Why: \(I = -I\).

Check by parts
\[I = -\int_{0}^{\pi} (\pi x - x^2)\cos x\,dx\]
\[\int_{0}^{\pi} \pi x\cos x\,dx = -2\pi,\quad \int_{0}^{\pi} x^2\cos x\,dx = -2\pi\]
Why: \(I = -(-2\pi - (-2\pi)) = 0\), using \(\int x\cos x = x\sin x + \cos x\) and \(\int x^2\cos x = x^2\sin x + 2x\cos x - 2\sin x\).

blocks.explanation:
Everything is written in terms of \(x - 2\), and 2 is the midpoint of \([1, 3]\).
Put \(t = x - 2\): the interval becomes \([-1, 1]\) and the integrand is odd in \(t\).
Property V then gives 0.
steps:
Given: \(I = \int_{1}^{3} \frac{(x - 2)^3 + 4(x - 2)}{1 + e^{(x - 2)^2}}\,dx\).
To prove: \(I = 0\).
Method: substitution \(t = x - 2\), then Property V (odd function on \([-a, a]\)).

Substitute \(t = x - 2\)
\[dt = dx,\quad x = 1 \Rightarrow t = -1,\quad x = 3 \Rightarrow t = 1\]
\[I = \int_{-1}^{1} \dfrac{t^3 + 4t}{1 + e^{t^2}}\,dt\]
Why: this centres the interval at 0.

Test odd or even
\[g(-t) = \dfrac{-t^3 - 4t}{1 + e^{t^2}} = -g(t)\]
Why: the top \(t^3 + 4t\) is odd and the bottom \(1 + e^{t^2}\) is even; odd divided by even is odd.

Apply Property V
\[I = \int_{-1}^{1} g(t)\,dt = 0\]
Why: an odd function on \([-1, 1]\) has integral 0.

Check
\[x = 1.5,\ 2.5\ \leftrightarrow\ t = \mp 0.5\]
Why: points mirrored about \(x = 2\) give opposite values of the integrand, so the areas cancel; a numerical evaluation gives 0.
